front: Who can act as importer of record (IOR) on a US entry?
back: The owner or purchaser of the goods, or a licensed customs broker designated by the owner, purchaser or consignee (19 U.S.C. 1484). The IOR must use reasonable care to enter, classify and value the goods.

front: What is a licensed customs broker?
back: A person or company licensed by the customs authority to transact customs business for importers: preparing and filing entries, paying duties and dealing with customs. US brokers are licensed by CBP under 19 CFR Part 111.

front: If our broker files and pays a US entry, who remains liable for the duties?
back: The importer. Duties are the importer's personal debt to the US (19 CFR 141.1). Paying the broker does not discharge it if the broker fails to pay CBP, and the customs bond does not relieve the importer either.

front: What is CBP's role in US imports?
back: U.S. Customs and Border Protection (part of DHS) releases goods, assesses and collects duties, taxes and fees, enforces trade laws, fixes final classification and value at liquidation, and operates ACE.

front: What is the CBSA's role in Canadian imports?
back: The Canada Border Services Agency releases imported goods, assesses and collects duties and taxes (including GST) through CARM, enforces border and trade laws, and licenses customs brokers.

front: How do ANAM and SAT divide responsibilities for Mexican imports?
back: ANAM (Agencia Nacional de Aduanas de México, operating since 1 Jan 2022 under SHCP) runs customs and collects foreign-trade duties. SAT remains the tax authority: RFC, e.firma, padrón de importadores and domestic taxes.

front: What is an agente aduanal?
back: A Mexican customs broker: an individual holding a government-issued patente who prepares and files pedimentos and clears goods on the importer's behalf. Broker firms are called agencias aduanales.

front: Why does our team audit what brokers file if brokers are licensed experts?
back: Because in all three countries the importer, not the broker, stays responsible for accurate declarations and duties. We supply the classification, value and origin data, so we must verify brokers declared it correctly.

front: What is the difference between a US entry and an entry summary?
back: The entry (cargo release, CBP Form 3461 data) asks CBP to release the goods. The entry summary (CBP Form 7501 data) declares classification, value and origin and deposits estimated duties. They can be filed together.

front: When is a US entry summary due if it is not filed at the time of entry?
back: Within 10 working days after the time of entry, with estimated duties attached (19 CFR 142.12(b)).

front: What does US entry type 01 mean?
back: Consumption entry, free and dutiable: the standard formal entry for commercial goods entering US commerce.

front: What does US entry type 11 mean?
back: Informal entry, free and dutiable: a simplified entry for low-value shipments, generally US$2,500 or less (19 CFR 143.21, as of 2026). Quota and AD/CVD goods, among others, still require formal entry.

front: What is ACE?
back: The Automated Commercial Environment: CBP's single-window system for processing US imports and exports. Brokers file entries into it, and importers can run reports on their own entries in the ACE Portal.

front: What is ABI?
back: The Automated Broker Interface: the electronic (EDI) channel that brokers and self-filing importers use to transmit entries and entry summaries into ACE, built to CBP's CATAIR specifications.

front: What is liquidation of a US entry?
back: CBP's final computation (ascertainment) of the duties, taxes and fees owed on an entry. After liquidation, changes generally need a protest rather than a post-summary correction.

front: When do most US entries liquidate in practice?
back: About 314 days after the date of entry: ACE schedules automatic liquidation then unless liquidation is extended or suspended. Check the actual scheduled date in ACE.

front: What is the statutory deadline for CBP to liquidate a US entry?
back: One year from the date of entry (19 U.S.C. 1504), extendable to a maximum of four years. If CBP misses it, the entry is deemed liquidated at the rate, value and amount the importer declared.

front: What is a Post-Summary Correction (PSC)?
back: An electronic correction to an accepted, unliquidated entry summary, filed through ACE, e.g., to fix classification, value or a preference claim. It can increase or decrease the duty owed.

front: What is the filing window for a Post-Summary Correction?
back: Within 300 days from the date of entry and no later than 15 days before the scheduled liquidation date, whichever is earlier. After liquidation, use a protest or prior disclosure instead.

front: How long does an importer have to file a US protest?
back: 180 days after the date of liquidation (or of the decision protested) for entries made on or after 18 Dec 2004 (19 CFR 174.12). File in ACE or on CBP Form 19.

front: What does reasonable care require of a US importer?
back: A legal duty (19 U.S.C. 1484, from the 1993 Mod Act) to use care in entering, classifying and valuing goods and giving CBP accurate information. Relying on a broker does not transfer this duty.

front: What is a US prior disclosure?
back: Telling CBP about a customs violation (19 U.S.C. 1592) before, or without knowledge of, a formal investigation, and paying the lost duties. It substantially reduces penalties (19 CFR 162.74).

front: What is a US customs bond?
back: A surety contract guaranteeing CBP that duties, taxes and fees will be paid and entry obligations met. A single transaction bond covers one entry; a continuous bond covers all entries for a year and renews.

front: What is ISF '10+2'?
back: Importer Security Filing for US-bound ocean cargo: the importer files 10 data elements (e.g., seller, buyer, manufacturer, country of origin, HTS-6) at least 24 hours before lading abroad; the carrier files 2 (stow plan, container status messages).

front: How long must US import records be kept?
back: Five years from the date of entry (19 CFR 163.4), with exceptions; e.g., drawback records are kept until three years after the claim is paid.

front: How long must Canadian import records be kept?
back: Six years following the importation of commercial goods, normally at the importer's place of business in Canada (Imported Goods Records Regulations; CBSA Memorandum D17-1-21).

front: How long must Mexican import records generally be kept?
back: Generally five years: the Código Fiscal de la Federación (art. 30) sets five years and defers to customs law for import documents. Confirm program-specific rules (e.g., IMMEX) with the agente aduanal or counsel.

front: How long must an importer claiming USMCA preference keep records?
back: At least five years from the date of importation, including the certification of origin relied on (USMCA Art. 5.8). National law can require longer, e.g., Canada's six years.

front: What is the primary customs valuation method in the US, Canada and Mexico?
back: Transaction value: the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to the importing country, plus specified additions. All three follow the WTO Customs Valuation Agreement.

front: What are the five statutory additions to US transaction value?
back: If not already in the price: packing costs, selling commissions paid by the buyer, assists, royalties or license fees paid as a condition of sale, and resale proceeds accruing to the seller.

front: What is an assist in customs valuation?
back: Something the buyer supplies free or at reduced cost for producing the imported goods: materials or components, tools/dies/molds, merchandise consumed in production, or engineering/design work done outside the US (19 CFR 152.102).

front: Why are assists a data risk for a BSA?
back: Their value must be added to the declared customs value, but they rarely appear on the supplier invoice or PO (e.g., molds we paid for), so value data built only from purchase prices understates value.

front: Which costs are excluded from US transaction value if separately identified?
back: International freight and insurance, post-importation construction, assembly or maintenance charges, and US duties and federal taxes owed because of importation.

front: Which of the three countries values imports on a CIF basis?
back: Mexico: customs value includes freight, insurance and related costs up to the point of entry. The US excludes international freight; Canada excludes transport from the place of direct shipment to Canada.

front: Can transaction value be used for related-party purchases?
back: Yes, if the relationship did not influence the price (shown by the circumstances of sale) or the price closely approximates a test value. The importer must be able to show this.

front: What is an ad valorem duty?
back: A duty charged as a percentage of the goods' customs value, e.g., X% of value.

front: What is a specific duty?
back: A duty charged per physical unit, e.g., cents per kilogram, per dozen or per liter, regardless of the goods' value.

front: What is a compound duty?
back: A duty that combines an ad valorem and a specific component on the same tariff line, e.g., X% of value plus Y cents per kilogram.

front: What is the US Merchandise Processing Fee (MPF)?
back: A CBP user fee on formal entries, charged ad valorem on customs value, with a minimum and maximum per entry that CBP adjusts every fiscal year (19 CFR 24.23). Check current amounts before modeling.

front: What is the US Harbor Maintenance Fee (HMF)?
back: An ad valorem fee on commercial cargo loaded or unloaded at covered US ports. It applies to vessel shipments only, not air, truck or rail, and has no minimum or cap (19 CFR 24.24).

front: Do USMCA-originating goods pay the US MPF?
back: No: originating goods properly claimed under USMCA are exempt from MPF. MPF already paid is not refunded through a post-importation USMCA claim.

front: What do the HTSUS rate columns 1-General, 1-Special and 2 mean?
back: 1-General: normal trade relations (MFN) rate. 1-Special: preferential rates under trade programs and FTAs, flagged by program codes. 2: statutory rates for countries without normal trade relations.

front: What is the IGI in Mexico?
back: Impuesto General de Importación: Mexico's general import duty, with rates set by 8-digit fracción arancelaria in the TIGIE and calculated mainly on customs value.

front: How is IVA on a Mexican import calculated?
back: On customs value plus IGI and the other import contributions such as DTA (Ley del IVA art. 27). It is paid on the pedimento and is generally creditable for the importer.

front: How is GST on a commercial import into Canada calculated?
back: CBSA collects it at importation on the value for tax: value for duty plus customs duties and other duties and taxes (excluding GST). GST registrants can generally claim it back as an input tax credit.

front: What is the Harmonized System (HS)?
back: The World Customs Organization's international product nomenclature, harmonized at the 6-digit level. Countries add national digits beyond six for their own tariffs and statistics.

front: How is the HS organized from broadest to narrowest?
back: Sections (groups of chapters), then 2-digit chapters, 4-digit headings and 6-digit subheadings. Example: 8471.30 is chapter 84, heading 84.71, subheading 8471.30.

front: How often is the HS amended, and when does the next edition apply?
back: Normally about every five years. The next edition, HS 2028, takes effect 1 January 2028, so national tariffs and item-master classifications must be remapped.

front: How many digits is a US HTSUS number and what do they mean?
back: Ten: the 8-digit subheading is the legal tariff line where the duty rate is set; the last 2 digits are a statistical suffix used for trade statistics.

front: How is a Canadian tariff classification number structured?
back: Ten digits: 6 HS digits plus 2 Canadian digits form the 8-digit tariff item, where duty rates are set; the last 2 digits are a statistical suffix.

front: How is a Mexican tariff classification code structured?
back: An 8-digit fracción arancelaria in the TIGIE (6 HS + 2 Mexican digits; sets the duty) plus a 2-digit NICO (Número de Identificación Comercial), in use since 28 December 2020.

front: Does a US 10-digit HTS number carry over to Canada or Mexico?
back: No. Only the first 6 HS digits are harmonized; digits 7-10 are set independently by each country, so each country's code must be classified and maintained separately.

front: What are the General Rules of Interpretation (GRIs)?
back: Six legally binding rules for classifying goods in the HS and national tariffs. They are applied in numerical order; once a rule settles the classification, later rules are not used.

front: What does GRI 1 say?
back: Classification is determined by the terms of the headings and any relevant section or chapter notes. Section and chapter titles are for reference only. Most goods are classified at GRI 1.

front: What does GRI 2(a) cover?
back: Incomplete or unfinished articles that have the essential character of the finished article, and complete articles presented unassembled or disassembled, are classified as the complete, finished article.

front: What does GRI 2(b) cover?
back: A heading's reference to a material or substance includes mixtures or combinations of it with other materials. Goods of more than one material are then classified under GRI 3.

front: What does GRI 3(a) say?
back: When goods are prima facie classifiable under two or more headings, the heading with the most specific description is preferred over headings with a more general description.

front: What does GRI 3(b) say?
back: Mixtures, composite goods and sets put up for retail sale that GRI 3(a) cannot resolve are classified by the material or component that gives them their essential character.

front: What does GRI 3(c) say?
back: When GRI 3(a) and 3(b) cannot decide, classify under the heading that occurs last in numerical order among those that equally merit consideration.

front: What does GRI 4 say?
back: Goods that cannot be classified under GRIs 1 to 3 are classified under the heading for the goods to which they are most akin. It is rarely used.

front: What does GRI 5 cover?
back: Containers. 5(a): specially shaped cases suitable for long-term use (e.g., camera or instrument cases) presented with their articles classify with them. 5(b): normal packing classifies with the goods unless clearly suitable for repetitive use.

front: What does GRI 6 say?
back: Subheadings are determined by their terms and any subheading notes, applying GRIs 1-5 by analogy and comparing only subheadings at the same level (one-dash with one-dash).

front: What is the purpose of HTSUS Chapter 98?
back: Special classification provisions, e.g., US goods returned (9801) or articles assembled abroad from US components (9802), which can give duty relief if their conditions and documentation requirements are met.

front: What is the purpose of HTSUS Chapter 99?
back: Temporary legislation, temporary modifications and additional import restrictions, e.g., Section 301 and 232 duties. Chapter 99 numbers are reported in addition to the Chapter 1-97 classification, never on their own.

front: What is CROSS?
back: CBP's Customs Rulings Online Search System (rulings.cbp.gov): a searchable database of CBP Headquarters and New York rulings from 1989 on, cross-referenced to later modifications and revocations.

front: What is a US binding ruling?
back: A written CBP decision under 19 CFR Part 177, normally requested before import, applying the law to a specific described transaction. CBP must follow it until modified or revoked, if the facts given were accurate.

front: Can we rely on a CROSS ruling issued to another importer?
back: Only as guidance. Under 19 CFR 177.9 a ruling covers the transaction it describes, and others should not assume it applies. Confirm the facts match, or request our own ruling.

front: What are the HS Explanatory Notes?
back: The WCO's official interpretation of the HS at the international level, describing each heading's scope, inclusions and exclusions. They are not part of the legal text; the US treats them as persuasive, not binding.

front: What is CARM?
back: CBSA Assessment and Revenue Management: CBSA's system for assessing and collecting duties and taxes on commercial imports. It became the official system of record on 21 October 2024.

front: What is the CARM Client Portal (CCP)?
back: CBSA's online portal where importers register their business, delegate access to customs brokers, enrol in programs such as RPP, post financial security and view statements of account.

front: What replaced the B3 in Canada?
back: The Commercial Accounting Declaration (CAD), from 21 October 2024 under CARM. It replaced the B3-3 coding form and the B2 adjustment request; adjustments are submitted as new versions of the CAD.

front: What account numbers does a business need to import commercial goods into Canada?
back: A 9-digit Business Number (BN) plus an import-export (RM) program account, e.g., 123456789RM0001. RM accounts are registered through the CARM Client Portal.

front: What are CBSA D-Memoranda?
back: CBSA's departmental memoranda (series D1 to D23) explaining how it applies customs legislation, regulations and policy, e.g., D10 classification, D13 valuation, D17 accounting. They are guidance, not law.

front: What is Release Prior to Payment (RPP) in Canada?
back: A CBSA program that releases goods before duties and taxes are paid, with payment due later on the monthly statement of account. Importers must enrol and post financial security.

front: Can a Canadian importer rely on its customs broker's security for RPP?
back: No. Since the CARM transition ended (20 May 2025), importers must post their own financial security in CARM; without it, duties and taxes are payable at release.

front: What is Canada's reason-to-believe correction obligation?
back: Under Customs Act s. 32.2, an importer with reason to believe an origin, tariff classification or value for duty declaration is incorrect must correct it and pay any duties owing within 90 days.

front: What is a pedimento?
back: Mexico's customs declaration, normally transmitted electronically by the agente aduanal, declaring the goods, tariff code, value, origin, customs regime and taxes paid (e.g., IGI, DTA, IVA). It is the core import record.

front: What is Anexo 22 of Mexico's foreign-trade rules (RGCE)?
back: The instructions for completing the pedimento, including appendices (catalogues) of codes, e.g., customs offices, pedimento keys (A1 = definitive import), regimes and countries, that every pedimento must use.

front: What is the padrón de importadores?
back: Mexico's mandatory importer registry (Ley Aduanera art. 59-IV), managed through SAT. Registration requires an active RFC, a valid e.firma and tax compliance; some goods also need a sector-specific padrón.

front: What is the RFC?
back: Registro Federal de Contribuyentes: Mexico's federal taxpayer ID issued by SAT. The importer's RFC is declared on the pedimento and must be active to stay in the padrón de importadores.

front: What is the e.firma?
back: SAT's advanced electronic signature (formerly FIEL): personal, non-transferable credentials used to sign filings such as padrón requests, broker authorizations and electronic value declarations.

front: What is VUCEM?
back: Mexico's foreign-trade single window (Ventanilla Única de Comercio Exterior Mexicana) for permits, electronic value documents (COVE) and other trade filings. A May 2026 decree created a successor window run by ATDT; confirm current naming.

front: What is the TIGIE?
back: Mexico's import and export tariff schedule, contained in the Ley de los Impuestos Generales de Importación y de Exportación (LIGIE). It sets IGI rates by 8-digit fracción arancelaria.

front: When did USMCA enter into force?
back: 1 July 2020, replacing NAFTA.

front: What are USMCA's names in each country?
back: USMCA in the US, CUSMA in Canada (Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement) and T-MEC in Mexico (Tratado entre México, Estados Unidos y Canadá). All refer to the same agreement.

front: What are the four USMCA origin criteria (A to D)?
back: A: wholly obtained or produced in the region. B: meets the Annex 4-B product-specific rule using non-originating materials. C: made exclusively from originating materials. D: narrow parts/unassembled-goods case meeting a regional value content test.

front: What is a tariff shift rule of origin?
back: A product-specific rule requiring each non-originating material to change tariff classification (chapter, heading or subheading) through production in the region, e.g., 'a change to heading X from any other heading'.

front: What is the USMCA transaction value formula for regional value content (RVC)?
back: RVC = (TV - VNM) / TV x 100, where TV is the good's transaction value adjusted to exclude international shipping costs and VNM is the value of non-originating materials.

front: What is the USMCA net cost formula for regional value content (RVC)?
back: RVC = (NC - VNM) / NC x 100, where NC is total cost minus sales promotion, marketing, after-sales service, royalty, shipping and packing, and non-allowable interest costs.

front: What is the USMCA de minimis rule?
back: A good can still qualify if non-originating materials that fail the required tariff shift are worth no more than 10% of the good's transaction value or total cost (Art. 4.12), subject to exceptions; textiles use weight.

front: What is accumulation under USMCA?
back: Originating materials from one USMCA country count as originating when used in another, and production by several producers across the region can be combined to meet the origin rules (Art. 4.11).

front: Who may complete a USMCA certification of origin?
back: The importer, the exporter or the producer (Art. 5.2). Mexico began accepting importer certifications on 1 January 2024, after its transition period.

front: Is there a mandatory form for a USMCA certification of origin?
back: No. Any format works, including an invoice, if it contains the nine minimum data elements in Annex 5-A; electronic signatures are allowed. NAFTA's CBP Form 434 is no longer used.

front: What are the nine minimum data elements of a USMCA certification of origin?
back: 1 certifier role (importer, exporter or producer); 2 certifier; 3 exporter; 4 producer; 5 importer; 6 description and 6-digit HS classification; 7 origin criterion; 8 blanket period; 9 authorized signature and date.

front: What period can a USMCA blanket certification cover?
back: Multiple shipments of identical goods within the period stated on the certification, which may not exceed 12 months.

front: How long must customs accept a USMCA certification of origin?
back: Four years after the date it was completed (USMCA Chapter 5). This acceptance period is separate from the five-year recordkeeping requirement.

front: How does a US importer claim USMCA preference at entry?
back: By holding a valid certification of origin when the claim is made and prefixing the HTSUS number with special program indicator 'S' (or 'S+' where applicable) on the entry summary.

front: Can a US importer claim USMCA preference after entry if it did not claim at entry?
back: Yes: a post-importation claim under 19 U.S.C. 1520(d) within one year of importation, with a certification of origin. CBP cannot extend the deadline, and MPF paid is not refunded.

front: What is the USMCA joint review?
back: Under Art. 34.7 the Free Trade Commission meets on the sixth anniversary of entry into force (2026), and each Party confirms in writing whether it wants to extend the 16-year term for another 16 years.

front: What happens if not every USMCA Party confirms extension at the joint review?
back: The agreement stays in force; the Commission holds annual joint reviews for the rest of the term, and the Parties can still confirm extension. Without it, USMCA terminates 16 years after entry into force (2036).
